proofs.full_local_argument: This entire argument is local reconstruction, not source text. Translate the candidate to (0,0), write f0=f(0,0), and use Euclidean norms and induced matrix norms. First-order necessity: Definition 14 gives f(0,v)<=f0 for all sufficiently small v, hence grad_y f(0,0)=0. Put g=grad_x f(0,0). For nonzero sufficiently small u let delta=||u|| and select a maximizer v_u over ||v||<=h(delta). Continuity and compactness give existence; shrinking delta ensures this ball lies in the domain. Definition 14 gives f(u,v_u)>=f0 and ||v_u||<=h(||u||)->0. Local maximality gives f(0,v_u)<=f0. Thus 0<=f(u,v_u)-f0<=f(u,v_u)-f(0,v_u). Integrating the x gradient along the segment, the last difference is g^T u+e(u), where |e(u)|<=||u|| sup_{0<=t<=1}||grad_x f(tu,v_u)-g||=o(||u||). For each unit a take u=t a and u=-t a and let t decrease to zero; both inequalities force g^T a=0. Therefore g=0. Second-order necessity: twice total differentiability on a neighborhood gives C1 there and the first-order conclusion. At the candidate the symmetric Hessian yields f(u,v)-f0=Q(u,v)+r(u,v), Q(u,v)=(1/2)u^T A u+u^T C v+(1/2)v^T B v, with r(u,v)=o(||u||^2+||v||^2). Setting u=0 and using local maximality along every direction gives B negative semidefinite. Now assume B negative definite and choose b>0 with v^T B v<=-b||v||^2. Use the same v_u as above, so both u and v_u tend to zero. In a sufficiently small neighborhood |r(u,v)|<=epsilon(||u||^2+||v||^2) with epsilon<=min(1,b/4). Put a0=||A||/2+1 and c=||C||. Since f(u,v_u)-f0>=0, 0<=a0||u||^2+c||u||||v_u||-(b/4)||v_u||^2. For u nonzero, z=||v_u||/||u|| satisfies (b/4)z^2-cz-a0<=0, so z is bounded by a finite constant independent of small u. Hence r(u,v_u)=o(||u||^2). Set D=B^{-1}C^T and S=A-C B^{-1}C^T. Completing the square gives Q(u,v)=(1/2)u^T S u+(1/2)(v+Du)^T B(v+Du)<=(1/2)u^T S u. Consequently 0<=f(u,v_u)-f0<=(1/2)u^T S u+o(||u||^2). Set u=t a, divide by t^2, and let t decrease to zero to obtain a^T S a>=0 for every a. Strict sufficiency: assume stationarity, B negative definite and S positive definite. Choose b,s>0 with B<=-b I and S>=s I. Taylor expansion gives f(0,v)-f0<=-(b/4)||v||^2 for all sufficiently small v. Set D=B^{-1}C^T, k=max(1,||D||), and h(delta)=k delta. For every ||u||<=delta choose v=-Du, which satisfies ||v||<=h(delta). Direct substitution gives Q(u,-Du)=(1/2)u^T S u. Since ||(u,-Du)||^2<=(1+||D||^2)||u||^2, the Taylor remainder is o(||u||^2) uniformly along these displacements. Choose delta0 small enough that |r(u,-Du)|<=(s/4)||u||^2 for all 0<||u||<=delta0 and that the required product balls lie in the domain. Then f(u,-Du)-f0>=(s/4)||u||^2>0 for nonzero u. For u=0 choose v=0 and obtain equality. Thus for every 0<delta<=delta0 and all ||u||<=delta, max_{||v||<=h(delta)}f(u,v)>=f0. Combined with f(0,v)<=f0 for ||v||<=delta this is Definition 14. The same h works for all admissible points and tends to zero, including when D=0. No Hessian continuity or external scientific lemma is used.

assumptions: Proposition 18: f is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood.

Propositions 19–20: f is twice differentiable on a neighborhood in the total derivative sense, giving a joint second-order Taylor expansion at the candidate. Existence of coordinate second partial derivatives alone is insufficient; Hessian continuity is not required.
statement.conclusion: Proposition 18: local minimax implies grad_x f=grad_y f=0. Proposition 19: local minimax implies B negative semidefinite; if B is negative definite then S is positive semidefinite. Proposition 20: stationarity together with B negative definite and S positive definite implies local minimax. The paper calls stationary points satisfying these strict Hessian inequalities strict local minimax points.
statement.objects_and_definitions: Let f be real-valued on an open neighborhood of (x*,y*) in R^{d_x} x R^{d_y}, with Euclidean norms. Local minimax means there exist delta0>0 and h:(0,delta0]->[0,infinity), h(delta)->0 as delta->0+, such that for every 0<delta<=delta0 and every x,y satisfying ||x-x*||<=delta and ||y-y*||<=delta, f(x*,y)<=f(x*,y*)<=max_{||y'-y*||<=h(delta)}f(x,y'). All sufficiently small required product balls lie in the domain. At the candidate write A=f_xx, B=f_yy, C=f_xy and, when B is negative definite, S=A-C B^{-1} C^T.
statement.parameter_domains: d_x,d_y are positive finite integers; delta0>0; 0<delta<=delta0; h(delta)>=0 with limit zero. B^{-1} is used only for B negative definite.
statement.quantifiers_and_randomness: For every such f and candidate the stated necessary conditions apply if it is local minimax. Conversely every stationary candidate satisfying the strict Hessian conditions is local minimax. The existential radius function is common to all admissible x,y and sufficiently small delta. All claims are deterministic.
